content:
Iambic Therapeutics (IAM) was just added to the Nasdaq Composite Index after a busy October that included its US$150 million IPO and a US$184.6 million shelf registration.

The recent Nasdaq Composite inclusion builds on a sharp positive swing in Iambic Therapeutics' trading, with a 1-day share price return of 25.91% and a year-to-date share price return of 48.81%, signalling strong upward momentum in a short time frame.

Capitalize on the momentum around Iambic Therapeutics by scanning a handpicked set of healthcare AI peers in the 33 healthcare AI stocks that could be setting up for their next move.

Iambic Therapeutics has just ripped higher after its IPO and index add, which leaves a practical fork in the road. Do you lean into this early AI‑driven biotech story now or wait for calmer prices before running the numbers?

Preferred multiple of price-to-book: Is it justified?

Iambic Therapeutics is trading on financials that are hard to slot into neat textbook ratios. The stock carries a P/B of -4.9x because the business currently has negative equity, while peers in the US Biotechs group sit at 1.9x on the same yardstick.

Price to book usually compares a company's market value with its net assets on the balance sheet. For a young biotech like Iambic Therapeutics, heavy R&D spending and cumulative losses can erode equity, so the ratio becomes distorted and less useful as a yardstick for what investors are really paying for pipeline potential.

The key point is that the market is not lining IAM up against the average US Biotechs P/B of 1.9x at all. With equity in a deficit, the quoted multiple does not give a clean read on what buyers are assuming about future trials, partnerships, or eventual cash generation.

That kind of profile is better tested against cash flow scenarios than balance sheet book value. This is why investors often look to a discounted cash flow approach when P/B turns negative. Look into how the SWS DCF model arrives at its fair value.

Still, the story around Iambic Therapeutics can change quickly if clinical data disappoints or if funding conditions tighten and further dilute existing shareholders.
